sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
Western Europe is four crowns and a republic, done with religious war and now rivals in ships, companies, credit, colonies and magic. Each crown has a minister of magic and licenses it; in 1668 each has just learned that it is behind. It is the setting's front door and the home of the Great Game.

**The one thing to remember:** in Western Europe magic is a state asset, and the crime isn't magic, it's unlicensed magic. Whoever writes the license holds the power, so a license is a weapon, and the Great Game is fought with them.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
Not one great forest: the lowlands were cleared centuries ago, and what woodland is left is managed, coppiced or royal hunting forest under its own law. The Hidden wait at the hedge, the ringfort and the parish edge, not in a wild wood.

- **The cold.** The Little Ice Age is at its depth (1668 sits inside the Maunder Minimum). Hard winters come in clusters; the Thames froze in four winters between 1649 and 1666.
- **The plague's tail.** London's Great Plague was 1665–66, and Basel's last outbreak is running now. Healers, druids and clerics are few, so magic blunts an epidemic, here and everywhere, without stopping it (see Powers and Factions, Lanternhall and the Healers).
- **The fens.** Investors and Dutch engineers are draining England's Fens; the fenmen, who fish and fowl there, break the dikes, and the drained peat shrinks and floods again.
- **The uplands.** Highland Scotland, Wales and western Ireland are open grazing. Wolves are gone from England but survive in the Highlands and Ireland.
- **Ireland**, the empire nearest home, is being remapped. Catholics held about 60% of its land in 1641, before Cromwell's conquest; the Down Survey (1656–58), walked mostly by former soldiers, mapped what was forfeited, and its maps, kept in Dublin, decided who got it.
- **The cities.** London had more than eighty coffeehouses by 1663, each a reading room, a post office and a rumor mill.

> *"The Thames froze again. The printers set up on the ice, and someone sold a Mutapan stove to warm the booth. It cost more than the press."* (a London stationer)

> **Further in.** The fenmen say the marsh had other tenants before the investors came.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
The courts' pattern is in Powers and Factions (The Crowns and the Churches): crowns that own their churches absorb magic, church-run states regulate it. What follows is who sits where in 1668, and what each license is.

- **France absorbs.** Louis XIV has ruled in person since 1661; Colbert runs finance, manufactures and the colonial companies, and his clerks in Paris keep the register of licenses, for which magic is one more manufacture. The crown-salaried Académie royale des sciences (1666) tests and recommends. The *cabinet noir* reads the post, and Rossignol's Great Cipher keeps the king's own. The Huguenots still have the Edict of Nantes. *The license:* a royal patent entered in Colbert's register.
- **England absorbs.** Charles II, restored in 1660, keeps an alchemical laboratory and inherits John Dee's legacy, which is why the English call Mutapa's speaking stones by the name of Dee's shew-stone. The Royal Society (1660) is a self-funded gentlemen's club, not a state body; magic belongs to a committee of the Privy Council, which borrows its Fellows for an expert eye. Scotland keeps its own Privy Council in Edinburgh, and its Kirk is a rival source of legitimacy, with its own ideas about who may practice. *The license:* a Privy Council warrant, and in Scotland the Kirk session's silence.
- **Spain regulates.** The last Spanish Habsburg, Charles II, is a child king under the regency of his mother, Mariana of Austria, and the crown has defaulted on its bankers again and again. The Inquisition's *Suprema* has required material evidence in witchcraft cases since 1614. The Archbishop of Toledo, Cardinal Pascual de Aragón, sits on the regency junta. *The license:* an entry in the Inquisition's register, which the crown then taxes; a Spanish practitioner answers to the Inquisition first.
- **Portugal** is independent again under the Braganzas, after sixty years under Spain's king. It has lost Malacca and Colombo to the Dutch and, in Euphonia, Sofala to Mutapa. Catherine of Braganza's dowry gave England Bombay and Tangier.
- **The Dutch Republic is pragmatic,** and burned England's fleet in the Medway in 1667. The States General and the provinces rule, not a king. Its weapons: the Amsterdam Wisselbank, whose bank guilder is Europe's unit of account; the VOC and WIC, private companies with the right to make war and build forts; and presses that print banned books under false imprints. *The license:* a city's, granted through a guild, and cheap.

> **Further in.** Here the VOC never built its station at the Cape. Mutapa holds it. Dutch ships call at Mauritius, which the Dutch resettled in 1664, and, when they must, at Mutapa's harbor under Table Mountain, where they pay like everyone else.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Western wizardry follows the Children of the Emerald Tablet, Hermetic schools entrenched in the universities (see Powers and Factions). The natural philosophers came out of the same programs, and the Children lead the charge against them.

- **The minister of magic.** Whatever his title, his job is the license: who may practice, teach, sell and heal (see Powers and Factions, The Crowns and the Churches). A licensing examiner carries *Detect Magic* and a list. Mutapan curiosities don't show up on it, which is one reason the examiners are worried.
- **The witch hunts** (see Powers and Factions, The Witch Hunts). England has hanged hundreds and will reach at least 500; Scotland has tried thousands, most of them women, and will reach nearly four thousand (its last great panic was 1661–62); Spain's Inquisition braked the burning after 1614.
- **The Romani** are hunted as vagrants more than as witches. France sends Romani men to the galleys (1666); Spain has banned the word *gitano*, Romani dress and the Romani language (1633); England has hanged Romani under its Egyptians Acts. Fortune-telling is charged as fraud. The old accusation that they steal children is false here too: when a child vanishes, look to the Hidden.
- **Cunning folk** are literate, often book-owning, and in our history mostly not the hunts' targets. Here the license has made them targets: the examiners have them on their lists, because they practice the same magic as the licensed, out past the institutions' reach.
- **Clerics.** Catholic and Protestant clerics cast exactly the same spells, for all the bloodshed between them (see Magic, Faith and Wisdom).
- **Lanternhall**, in Basel, is the first serious rival to the Church's healing, and the home of the Physician (see Powers and Factions, Lanternhall and the Healers). Its elf, Ilyanor Sael, is a licensing problem for every Church in the west (see Running Euphonia, Notable People).

> **Further in.** Basel's last plague (around 1665–70) killed the young poor; the mass grave under the old plague hospital averages seventeen years old. There were never enough healers, and the Hall has to choose whom it treats first. It chose the students' own families first, and the lower city knows.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Western Europe's Hidden go by many names, and people avoid saying any. The 1668 evidence is court records and a few believers' treatises; most "folklore" was collected in the 19th century.

- **The Good People.** The Good Neighbors, the Gentry, the People of Peace; in Irish, the *aos sí*, the people of the mounds. Farmers leave Ireland's 45,000 surviving ringforts, their houses, unplowed. Robert Kirk (1691–92) will call them "of middle nature between Man and Angel."
- **In the witch trials,** a healer says her skill came from the fairies, and the court recasts the fairies as the Devil. In 1662 Isobel Gowdie said she had feasted with the fairy king and queen, seen elf boys making arrowheads and learned a charm to become a hare.
- **"Seely"**, an old Scots word for blessed or lucky, names kinds of fairy, not a government; the two-court model is attested only from 1783 and 1819.
- **The taken.** Fairies take infants, and new mothers to nurse fairy children, and leave a sickly substitute.
- **Goblins** are the Hidden's soldiers, or something like it (see Peoples, The Hidden Folk).
- **The Wild Hunt** rides out of the Bordermarches under local names: Herne the Hunter, the Gabriel Hounds of the north, Gwyn ap Nudd and the *Cŵn Annwn* in Wales, the *Mesnie Hellequin* and *le Grand Veneur* in France, Arthur in Brittany, the *hueste antigua* in Castile. ("Wild Hunt" itself is Grimm's term, from 1835.)
- **Protections.** Iron in the cradle and the doorway; St John's wort and yarrow against them. Hawthorn and foxglove are theirs, and harming them invites revenge. Every parish has its Killer, and its own word for one.

> **Further in.** Old families on both sides of the Channel count a fairy among their forebears, and have reasons to keep the licensing office friendly.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The red alert.** Every court's minister of magic has studied the Mutapan curiosities in his city's drawing rooms and seen that Mutapa is about to pull out of reach (see The World in 1668, The Mark). Their intelligence services are moving.
- **The platina.** Spain has been throwing away the metal Mutapa runs on, in the Chocó, and its court has worked out what it is. Every court has heard of the gate at Toledo (see The World in 1668, The Mark), and if the Chocó is lightly held, any crown with a fleet can have it (see Adventures and Hooks, The Great Game).
- **The Treaty of Lisbon** was signed in February: Spain recognizes Portugal's independence, and Portugal recognizes Ceuta, loyal to Spain since 1640, as Spanish. The Council of Portugal's papers are being carted out of Madrid.
- **Aix-la-Chapelle.** France is ending the War of Devolution and will keep twelve Spanish Netherlands towns. In July, Versailles, still the king's pleasure house, will hold the Grand Divertissement royal.
- **The companies.** Bombay will pass to the English East India Company this year. Radisson and des Groseilliers' first Hudson's Bay voyage is fitting out. Barbados, under the first English slave code (1661), sends England most of its Caribbean sugar.

> **Further in.** In our history, England and France attack the Dutch Republic together four years from now, in 1672, the Dutch "disaster year."

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The first fleet to the Chocó.** Which crown sends it, under what flag, and whether Spain can stop it.
- **The license war.** In every court, the Children of the Emerald Tablet, the Invisible College, the Agitators and the anti-monarchists each want the pen that writes the licenses. A single revocation can tip a court.
- **The Dutch reckoning.** The Republic is rich, unloved and alone, and the Wisselbank holds half of Europe's credit. Whoever breaks it breaks everyone's.
- **Lanternhall's graduates** are going home to countries whose Churches haven't licensed them, and the first hanging of a Lanternhall doctor will be a diplomatic incident.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The missing child.** A village blames a Romani family for a child the Hidden took, and the magistrate sits on Monday. Someone has to find the child, or the hill, before then.
- **The ringfort.** A Down Survey grantee has ordered a ringfort plowed, and the plowman has walked off the job. The grantee is paying well for men who don't believe in anything.
- **The coffeehouse.** A Mutapan stove in a London coffeehouse has stopped working, and the man who came to retune it was seen leaving with the owner's ledger.
- **The Fens.** A dike breaks on a night the fenmen swear they were home, and the Dutch engineer wants to know who else is breaking them.
- **The register.** A clerk in Colbert's licensing office has been selling entries, and one of them is in a dead man's name. The dead man's license is still being used.
- **The Ceuta papers.** The Council of Portugal's archive is on carts to Lisbon, and one cart holds the old register of Portuguese licenses, with names some families would rather forget.

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
Between France and the Urals, from Sicily to the North Cape, nobody is in charge. The Empire is hundreds of territories under an elected emperor. Poland–Lithuania elects its king, and one deputy can void a parliament. Sweden has a regency and Venice its councils; Italy has Spain, the Pope and a few dynasties. Russia is the exception, and it is splitting over how to make the sign of the cross.

**The one thing to remember:** where authority is divided or weak, the witch hunts burn. With no single hand on the license, every prince, bishop and village court decides for itself what counts as unlicensed magic.

> **Further in.** The Empire's largest witch hunts were in lands ruled by bishops, where the man who licensed magic and the man who judged it were the same man.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
- **The forests that are left.** The big forests are here: the German uplands, the Alps, the Carpathians, Poland–Lithuania and Russia, and even these are being cut for ships, charcoal and mine props.
- **The Black Forest** is being floated down the Neckar and the Rhine to Dutch shipyards and canal piles, on rafts over 1,000 feet long with crews of up to 500. Its oaks are disappearing.
- **The scars of the war.** The Thirty Years' War (1618–48) killed 4.5 to 8 million, mostly civilians, mostly by disease and hunger; some German regions lost over half their people, counting those who fled.
- **The Alps.** Summer pastures and mule passes. Glaciers are advancing on farms, and villages answer with processions and exorcisms.
- **Venice's lagoon** is always silting up. The Republic diverts whole rivers to keep it water.
- **The plains.** Sand, heath, bog and rye from the Netherlands to Russia; to the south-east, the Hungarian plain on the Ottoman frontier, and the Pontic steppe of Cossack, Tatar and Nogai herds.
- **The north.** Sápmi's fells and forests, reindeer country over three crowns' borders, Denmark–Norway's fishing stations out to Hammerfest and the long winter dark.
- **Animals.** The last aurochs died in a Polish royal forest in 1627. Wolves are common; bears are in every mountain range and the east.
- **Disease.** Plague is ending (Venice's last was 1630–31).

> **Further in.** A Black Forest fir felled in 1668 can end up as a pile under an Amsterdam canal house. Nobody asks the forest. Something in it is keeping count.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
This region is the third of the postures in Powers and Factions (The Crowns and the Churches), divided authority, with Rome and Russia as exceptions.

- **The Empire.** An elected Habsburg emperor in Vienna; eight electors; and since 1663 a permanent Imperial Diet at Regensburg, a congress of envoys. Each prince chose his territory's religion, now frozen as it stood in 1624, and each licenses magic in his own lands. Vienna's minister answers for the Habsburg lands, and the Diet argues about the rest. Brandenburg's Great Elector is building an army and taking his Estates' powers away from them.
- **The Habsburg frontier.** Hungary is split three ways: Habsburg Royal Hungary, Ottoman Hungary and Transylvania, an Ottoman tributary guaranteeing four religions and leaving out the Orthodox. The Military Frontier is a belt of armed refugee colonists, many Vlach and Serb, holding land for permanent border service.
- **Venice.** The doge has little power; the councils have it. The Council of Ten runs security and espionage, with three State Inquisitors, "lion's mouth" boxes for written denunciations and a cipher bureau a century ahead of its rivals. Venice sells noble rank to pay for the Cretan War. In Venice the Ten license magic, and a denunciation is how a license is lost.
- **Rome** is a court among courts, its prestige resting on faith. The Holy Office has prosecuted learned magic and astrology since 1586, and the Index bans the books. The Holy Office also keeps scholars who study what it bans, on the grounds that someone must.
- **The rest of Italy.** Medici Tuscany is scholarly, though its Accademia del Cimento has just closed. Genoa's bankers financed Spain for a century and still hold its paper. Naples, Sicily (from Palermo) and Milan have Spanish viceroys, and Naples remembers Masaniello's rising of 1647.
- **Sweden**'s empire of 2.5 million people is governed from Stockholm by a regency for the boy king Charles XI; its former queen, Christina, abdicated, converted and lives in Rome.
- **Denmark–Norway** became one of Europe's most absolute monarchies under the Lex Regia of 1665, and lives on the Sound Dues, a toll on every ship through the Øresund.
- **Sápmi**, the Sámi north, is taxed by Sweden, Denmark–Norway and Russia, sometimes all three in one winter. Sweden's church is pressing in: a school at Lycksele since 1632, drums seized, noaidi questioned. At Nasafjäll the crown forced Sámi to haul silver ore until the mine burned in 1659, and many fled to Norway.
- **The Romani of the east** live under other rules. In Wallachia and Moldavia they are enslaved, owned by princes, boyars and monasteries; in Hungary and Transylvania the diets pass no laws against them and protect their smiths and their voivodes.
- **Poland–Lithuania.** The *szlachta*, about a tenth of the people, rule through the Sejm at Warsaw. The Deluge (1655–60) cost a third of the population; the Truce of Andrusovo (1667) gave Russia left-bank Ukraine. South lie the Cossack Hetmanate, in the years called the Ruin, and the Crimean Tatars' slave raids.
- **Russia.** Tsar Alexei rules from Moscow, and licenses as the church directs. The 1666–67 councils deposed Patriarch Nikon but anathematized the old rite, and the Old Believers would rather burn than change how they cross themselves. Siberia, reached over the Urals by the road from Solikamsk, runs on river forts and forced fur tribute, against continuing resistance; epidemics have killed up to four-fifths of some Tungus and Yakut groups.

> **Further in.** One of the few platinum deposits that could match the Great Dyke is at Norilsk, in Arctic Siberia, where Russian fur traders and tribute collectors are just arriving.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
- **The hunts.** Germany has over half of Europe's witch trials, the worst in prince-bishoprics like Trier, Würzburg, Bamberg and Eichstätt (thousands burned between them in 1617–31). Torture produced chains of accusation; a Jesuit's anonymous *Cautio Criminalis* (1631) attacked the procedure and helped end the trials in Mainz. Here the hunts find real witches, and also anyone a neighbor names.
- **Prague's legacy.** Rudolf II's court kept Dee and Kelley, and later Tycho and Kepler, and imprisoned Kelley when his alchemy failed. Here their crystals worked, and Dee's "shew-stone" gave Mutapa's speaking stones their English name.
- **Learned spirits.** Agricola, founder of mineralogy, wrote up the mine spirits as mining science; Paracelsus classified the elementals (gnomes, undines, sylphs, salamanders), and in 1668 his book is widely read.
- **The night battles.** In Venetian Friuli the caul-born *benandanti* said their spirits left their bodies on the Ember Days to fight witches over the harvest, armed with fennel stalks. The Inquisition slowly turned them into witches.
- **The ladies from outside.** In Spanish Sicily, healers joined the *donne di fuora*, fairy companies under a Prince; the Inquisition mostly treated them as deluded.
- **Kabbalists** can be wizards, Envoy warlocks or both. In Venice's ghetto a golem walks after dark, and Simon Horowitz is trying to read a book an archangel gave him (see Running Euphonia, Notable People).
- **The noaidi's drum** is a working instrument of divination: rings on the skin, a bone hammer, a trance and a report on what was learned. Christian IV made Sámi drumming a capital crime in Denmark–Norway in 1609. In the hunts it is unlicensed magic, not a fae gift.

> *"The bishop's court wanted names. I gave them the woman who sold me a charm that worked. They burned her, and I still have the charm."* (a Franconian miller)

> **Further in.** In Venice, the Council of Ten drowned its condemned in the lagoon, in secret, which is one more reason the lagoon has things in it.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Every part of this region has its Hidden folk, but the 1660s record is thin, mostly church condemnations and trials; the detail is 19th-century. Slavic, Alpine and Scandinavian customs are alive and contradict one another.

- **The mine folk.** Kobolds help and hinder in houses and mines; Agricola's *Bergmännlein* look like old miners, laugh, throw pebbles and can lead a miner to silver. A troublesome ore, *kobelt*, was named after them, and cobalt is named for it.
- **The wild folk.** The hairy *wilder Mann*; the Tyrolean *Saligen Fräulein*, "blessed maidens"; Rübezahl, the weather spirit of the Riesengebirge, in print from 1662.
- **The leshy** is the master of a Slavic forest: as tall as the trees inside it and as short as the grass outside. The forest's edge is the edge of his power, which makes the village edge literal here.
- **The rusalka** is a water spirit, the soul of a drowned girl or unbaptized child, who dances in the birches at the start of summer; join the ring and you dance to death.
- **The domovoi** lives by the oven, and a family moving house has to invite him along.
- **The North.** Underground people, the forest *huldra*, the fiddling *näck*, the farm's *tomte* (mostly collected later).
- **The Wild Hunt** here is Wodan's *Wütendes Heer*, led by Holda in the north and Perchta in the south, or by the cursed huntsman Hackelberg; in Norway it's the *Åsgårdsreia*.
- **Where the edge doesn't fit.** The steppe herders and the Sámi reindeer herders have no village edge, and their Hidden don't wait at one. The Sámi underground people, the *gufihtar*, keep herds of their own and move with the seasons too. They take children, and a taken child who refuses their food comes home. (unverified: when the gufihtar lore was first written down)

> **Further in.** At Blåkulla the children will say they were carried away at night to a feast inside a hill. The theology is the Devil's, but the shape is the Hidden's.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The Blåkulla panic begins.** In Härjedalen, Märet Jonsdotter's trial starts rumors that witches are carrying children to a sabbath at Blåkulla. In our history the panic runs eight years and sends about 280 people to their deaths, children among them; at Mora in August 1669, twenty-three adults will die on children's testimony.
- **Candia** is in the last full year of its 21-year siege; Venice is desperate, and desperate states make mistakes. The Ten are selling what they can (see Adventures and Hooks, The Venice Job).
- **The Solovetsky Monastery** refuses the new rite, and this year the tsar's siege begins.
- **Stenka Razin's Cossacks** are raiding the Caspian coast, Persia's included.
- **Poland's king,** John II Casimir, will abdicate in September, and an election is coming. (unverified)
- **The red alert.** A Viennese lady has a Mutapan lamp in her drawing room. The emperor's counsellors know what it means.

> **Further in.** In our history, Kara Mustafa reaches the walls of Vienna in 1683.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The witch panic and the north.** German pamphlets say Sweden wins its wars by Sámi sorcery, and the chancellor wants a scholar to prove otherwise (in our history, Schefferus's *Lapponia*, 1673). Here someone has to decide what's true, in a kingdom with a witch panic of its own.
- **The Polish election.** Every court has a candidate, and some of the electors can be bought with magic.
- **The Ottoman frontier.** Candia's fall frees an Ottoman army, and the next place it looks is Hungary.
- **The Old Believers** in Russia's forests and monasteries are choosing fire over the new rite, and a tsar's church that licenses magic is deciding what to call their holy men.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The drum in the cabinet.** A seized Sámi drum sits in a prince's cabinet of curiosities, and its owner's family can't make decisions without it. The drum has started moving its own rings.
- **Blåkulla.** A Swedish commissioner rides to Härjedalen to take the children's testimony and needs people who can tell a witch from the Hidden from a frightened child. What carries the children off, if anything, is each table's to decide.
- **The benandante.** A benandante before the Venetian Inquisition says he fought something on the Ember Days, and he has the wounds. The inquisitor wants to know what.
- **The Bergmännlein.** A Saxon mine has stopped finding silver since the new captain fired the old miner who left pebbles out, and the mine folk have started throwing them back.
- **The raft.** A Black Forest raft bound for Amsterdam has a log in it that nobody cut, and the raftsmen won't go on until it's off.
- **The Frontier.** A Military Frontier village of Serb colonists has its Killer, its Hunt and an Ottoman raiding party in the same week, and the Graz war council wants to know which killed the patrol.
- **The vote.** A Polish noble with a vote in the coming election has been offered a Mutapan lamp, a French pension and a Swedish license, and has started asking which is worth most.

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
Mutapa is the Shona empire that kept its mines: in our history a Mutapa king ceded them to Portugal in 1607, and here he didn't. Sixty years later his heirs rule the richest state in Africa, run it like a counting house and power it with a metal no one else knows how to use. It is the other player at the table in the Great Game.

**The one thing to remember:** Mutapa isn't a hidden kingdom; it's an open one with a secret. Everyone trades with it, and no one can copy it. In 1668, the people whose job it is to notice have noticed.

> **Further in.** What Mutapa sells is not what it has.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
A high plateau between the Zambezi and the Limpopo, mostly over 3,000 feet up: not jungle or endless savanna, but open woodland that goes bare in the dry season. People have farmed, herded and mined it for over a thousand years; none of it is wilderness.

- **Seasons.** Cool and dry (April to early August, with frost on the high plateau from mid-May), hot and dry (to October) and the rains (November to March), which decide the year. Late in the dry season the msasa trees put out new leaves in orange, bronze and red before the rains come.
- **The miombo.** Open woodland of msasa and munondo over thin grass and poor soil, with grassy wetlands, *vleis*, along the streams.
- **The granite country.** *Kopjes*, granite domes and boulder hills, stud the plateau; their natural slabs built Great Zimbabwe without mortar. In the Matobo Hills, near Khami, the boulders go on like a sea.
- **The Great Dyke.** A ridge of ultramafic rock runs about 340 miles down the country's spine. Only a few specialist plants grow on it, and they are how Mutapa found what is under it.
- **The Eastern Highlands.** Mountains on the coast side, wet with mist and dew, the highest over 8,500 feet.
- **The lowlands.** Tsetse fly and malaria in the Zambezi and Limpopo valleys kill cattle and strangers. The plateau states sit in the healthy high country, and anyone after Mutapa's gold crosses the fever country to reach it.
- **The coast.** Sofala's harbor, mangroves, the Sofala Bank fishery and the monsoon, which blows ships north half the year and south the other half.
- **The Cape.** A different country, more than a thousand miles away by sea: winter rain, fynbos, Table Mountain and Khoekhoe grazing (see What's Happening in 1668).

> *"Everyone who comes up from the coast expects Africa to be hot. Then the first frost comes, and they start asking where to buy a Mutapan stove."* (a Sofala innkeeper)

> **Further in.** In our history, from the late 1660s to about 1680, locusts, smallpox, measles and plague emptied the Mutapa lands, and wild animals moved back into abandoned villages. Here it is starting now.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
Powers and Factions (Mutapa's Institutions) has the crown, the mediums, the House of the Bird, the Mhizha Guild and the spymaster in full. Here is how they sit on the ground.

- **The crown.** The paramount ruler is the *Mwenemutapa*, and his commander, the *mukomohasha*, is also "captain of the gates." Mukombwe holds the throne, as he did in our history: history keeps its shape where magic didn't bend it.
- **The merchant houses** steer the king, and right now the shewstone house has his ear.
- **The mediums** speak for the royal dead. Later sources call these spirits *mhondoro*, "lions," and their mediums *svikiro*; each guards a spirit province and its rain. Here the spirits are real and answer. In the south-west, petitioners climb to the Matobo shrines, where Mwari, the creator, is said to speak as a voice from the rocks.
- **The great artificer**, Simbarashe Moyo, is alive, tired, wary of Europe and unhappy with how the court stewards his work (see Running Euphonia, Notable People).
- **The tributaries.** Mutapa's overlordship is a relationship renewed, not a border. Uteve, Manyika (in the eastern highlands) and Barwe keep their own dynasties and pay in grain, gold, labor on the royal fields (*zunde*) and one tusk of every elephant killed. A borrower of the king's cattle (*kuronzera*) keeps the milk but can't sell the cow, and is the king's man. Royal officials put out every hearth and relight it from the king's fire; refusing it is rebellion.
- **The Torwa** rule Butua, to the south-west, from a court that has left Khami (unverified), and are no one's tributary. Portuguese observers called Butua "the Mother of Gold," and said its people cared more for cattle than mines.
- **The Portuguese remnant.** The prazo heirs on the Zambezi around Tete lost their leases when Mutapa kept its mines; some kept their private armies of enslaved soldiers, the *achikunda*, and sell them to anyone. The old plateau fairs, the *feiras* (Dambarare, Masapa), are Mutapa's customs posts now, where foreign traders live by the king's leave and pay for the right to trade.
- **The Cape's own people.** Mutapa rules the Khoekhoen of the Cape the way Shona kings have always ruled neighbors: the chiefdoms nearest the harbor are tributaries, bound by lent cattle, the new fire lit each reign from the king's own and a tax on every trade. Further out, the Cochoqua and the Chainouqua take Mutapa's terms when it suits them and a Dutch or English captain's when it doesn't. The San hold the mountains and the dry country, in no one's ledger.

> **Further in.** In the 1590s a Portuguese friar in neighboring Teve watched a possessed man at the royal graves speak in the dead king's voice, asked about war, famine and rain.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Mutapan magic is artifice, and it runs on platinum. It isn't stronger than other magic. It's better made. Magic, Artifice and Electricity has the theory; Characters has the seven curiosities.

- **The catalyst.** Platinum isn't consumed, so a Mutapan device runs for years where a European enchantment burns out. It turns raw magic into current, doesn't corrode and calibrates: one device behaves exactly like the next. That means workshops instead of lone geniuses, and interchangeable parts a century early.
- **Small work for anyone, big work for the trained.** A Mutapan lamp lights itself for whoever owns it; a weapon, a flight pack or an Arc Gun needs a trained artificer, a **Mhizha** (Shona for a master craftsman, now the name of the whole art).
- **Mutapa doesn't sell the big work,** and the small work drifts out of calibration, so a foreign owner eventually needs Mutapan hands to retune it.
- **The curiosity.** Abroad, a curiosity is the status object of the day: the lamp in a Viennese drawing room that tells guests how far its owner's reach extends. At home it's a stove in an ordinary kitchen.
- **Shewstones.** Europe's speaking stones are sperrylite, a platinum mineral, and come from Mutapa as the king's gifts, never sold. His great artificer and his spymaster think it the most dangerous thing he has done (see The World in 1668, Words Across Distance).
- **The older magic.** The healers, mediums and readers of plants work Wisdom magic, the crown's by custom, as artifice is the guild's (see Powers and Factions, The Mhizha Guild).

> **Further in.** The platinum came to Mutapa through a druid reading the plants on the Dyke. What else the plants know is anyone's guess.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Southern Africa's Hidden go by their own names. Most of the record was written down in the last two centuries and projected back; the royal mediums are the exception.

- **The water-takers.** Shona *njuzu*, pool spirits, take a person under, feed them mud and raw fish and send some back as healers if the family doesn't mourn: here, one way an **Oceanus Revelator** is called.
- **The river people.** In Xhosa tradition, one called by the river is taken to a snake-guarded enclosure underwater, where a half-fish old woman embodies the clan's ancestors; they return on the third day, in white clay.
- **The wanderers.** A *shave*, the spirit of someone who died far from home, chooses a host and gives a skill: hunting, healing, dancing, fighting. Unlike an ancestor, it can be refused.
- **The small people.** The *abatwa* of Nguni tradition are tiny, touchy hunters of the grass and anthills, with fixed rules for greeting them. The image may partly remember the San, who were pushed off that country, so play the abatwa as spirits and never as a picture of a people.
- **The bargain.** *Umamlambo* is a river woman or snake bought for wealth and paid for with a parent's life.
- **The Cape's Hidden.** The Khoekhoe Water Snake that keeps the springs, and the rain-animals of the San, the bull and the cow of the rain: here, Hidden on the land's own terms. The San themselves are people, never fae, and much of what is written about their beliefs was taken down from ǀXam speakers in the 1870s and can't simply be read back onto 1668.
- **The new border.** Mutapa's cities are growing fast into country that was always someone else's, and on their edges modern artifice meets the oldest things in the land (see Adventures and Hooks, The Border). South of the equator the Wild Hunt rides through the southern dark half, the cool dry months.

> **Further in.** The Lobedu, far to the south, trace their royal line to a princess who fled Mutapa in the 16th century with the power to make rain. Their Rain Queens are still to come; the rain is already there.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The red alert,** from the other side (see Western Europe). Europe's intelligence services are moving, and Mutapa's spymaster, whom her agents call **Shiri**, is watching them with a tenth of their assets.
- **The platina.** The same metal lies in Spain's Chocó, in New Granada, and Spain knows it now (see Western Europe); the question is who moves first.
- **The Cape.** Mutapa holds Hoerikwaggo, its town under Table Mountain: the gate every European fleet must pass to reach the Indies, and the great flashpoint.
- **The cattle.** The Cape's winter rains defeat the plateau's summer crops, so a Mutapan Cape lives on ships and on Khoekhoe cattle, and the herders know it: they trade the old and the barren and keep the breeding stock.
- **The go-between.** A Khoekhoe woman about twenty-five years old, raised in the harbor town, speaks four languages and is the most useful person at the Cape to four powers. In our history Krotoa lost her husband and her place in 1668.
- **The sickness.** Locusts and the first outbreaks are reaching the plateau's villages, and the healers are choosing where to go.
- **The Rozvi.** In our history a herder, Changamire Dombo, gathered followers he called the Rozvi and rose against the crown in the 1680s. Here that break hasn't come.

> **Further in.** In our history, Dombo rose just as the plagues that emptied the Mutapa lands were ending.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **Who governs?** A merchant house's quarrel with a royal medium, and a dead king with opinions about shewstones.
- **The great artificer's choice** between his nation and his science, and whoever means to stop him (see Powers and Factions, The Mhizha Guild).
- **The Cape.** Dutch and English fleets in one bay, and a Mutapan harbor master who takes anyone's fee.
- **The plague years.** Where the healers go decides who stays loyal, on the plateau and at the Cape.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The far chiefdoms.** A Cochoqua chief takes an English captain's muskets and Mutapa's cattle in the same month, and both think he's theirs.
- **The man from Sofala.** A Khoekhoe interpreter trained at Mutapa's ports comes home angry about the grazing, and knows exactly how Mutapan arms fail.
- **The ship with the fever.** Smallpox, in our history, reached the Cape on a ship in 1713 and killed most of the Khoekhoen near it. A ship from Sofala has it in the hold now, and Mutapa has two healers at Hoerikwaggo. Whom they treat first decides what the Cape becomes.
- **The painter.** In the Cederberg a San painter is putting Mutapa's ships on a rock wall, and a lamp that lights itself, and something no one else saw arriving.
- **Thirty head a year.** A tribute herd driven to Hoerikwaggo for the fleet is short, the escort is late and the chief says the rest died of the cattle sickness.
- **The cairn.** A Mutapan road crew has been ordered to clear the travelers' cairns for a new road, and none of them will touch a stone.
- **The Monsoon Road** starts here: a ship, a cargo of curiosities and an ocean of people who want to see inside one (see Adventures and Hooks).

sections.heading: Playing Here
Open for Developers
sections.text:
- **The capital, by name:** its old town under the new, its quarters and workshops, and the suburbs on the border, as a city to run like Venice.
- **The shewstones' danger:** whether Mutapa can listen through them, who has worked it out and what the spymaster does about it.
- **The Wild Hunt in southern Africa:** what it looks like when it comes, who rides and how a Shona village, a Khoekhoe camp and a city suburb each tell a raid from the Hunt.
- **The Lobedu's rain:** what the princess took with her from Mutapa, and whether Mutapa wants it back.
- **The Cape from the Khoekhoe side:** the chiefdoms by name, the go-betweens and what the tributaries and the free chiefdoms each want from Mutapa.
- **The Torwa and Butua:** a rival plateau kingdom with its own gold, its own mediums and its own reasons to talk to Mutapa's enemies.
- **Backgrounds for the region:** a Khoekhoe go-between, a prazo heir's achikunda soldier, a medium's attendant.

data.name: The Ottomans and the Islamic West

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
In 1668 the Ottoman Empire matches or outstrips Europe. It holds the coasts of three continents, besieges Venetian Crete and already has what Europe is still arguing about: a chief astrologer at court, hospitals centuries old and a learned magic written in Arabic before Europe had one.

**The one thing to remember:** the Islamic world isn't behind Europe in magic; it's older at it. The fight here is between the Sufi lodges and the preachers who call their practice illicit innovation, and in 1666 the preachers won a round.

> **Further in.** The Emerald Tablet, the Hermetic text Europe's wizards are named for, first appears in Arabic.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
Plateaus more than desert: cold Anatolian and Iranian uplands with snowy winters, the cedar and oak of the Atlas and Zagros, and Yemen's monsoon terraces.

- **The cold.** The Little Ice Age hit here too. Cold and drought in the 1590s broke the system that fed Istanbul and the army, fed the Celali revolts and emptied Anatolian villages; the recovery is still incomplete.
- **The herders.** Turkmen and Yörük nomads move between winter lowlands and summer *yayla*; Bedouin graze the Syrian steppe.
- **The Nile.** Egypt lives on the summer flood, fed by Ethiopia's rains (see The Horn and the Nile). A reading at the Rawda Nilometer sets the year's taxes; a low Nile means famine.
- **Lions and locusts.** Lions in the Atlas, Mesopotamia and Iran; locust swarms that strip a district in hours.
- **Plague** is endemic, back from the ports every few years.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The Porte.** Sultan Mehmed IV, servant of the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, reigns; the Köprülü grand viziers run the state. Köprülü Mehmed exiled the militant preachers to Cyprus in 1656; his son Fazıl Ahmed is pressing the siege of Candia in person (unverified).
- **The janissaries** were Christian-born boys levied from the Balkans. The levy has faded, but the corps can still make and unmake sultans, and killed Osman II in 1622.
- **The minister of magic** is the chief astrologer, the *müneccimbaşı* (see Powers and Factions, Institutions Beyond Europe).
- **Egypt** has an Ottoman governor, but the beys rule: households of bought, trained and freed soldiers, split into the Faqāriyya and the Qāsimiyya.
- **The Regencies** of Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli are Ottoman on paper, self-governing military states in fact. In Algiers the janissary agha took power from the pasha in 1659, and the corsair captains' guild, the *taifa*, is a constitutional body; in Tunis the bey is beating the dey; Tripoli changes rulers by coup. "Barbary" is Europe's name for this coast, from "Berber" by way of "barbarian," not the coast's own.
- **Morocco** was never Ottoman. Mawlāy al-Rashīd of the ʿAlawī family took Fez in 1666 and is taking the rest. For decades the strongest state in the north was the Dilāʾ, a Sufi lodge with a library.
- **Persia**, Shiʿi and at peace with the Porte since 1639, when Baghdad stayed Ottoman, has its own chapter (see Safavid Persia).
- **The conquered.** Balkan Christians gave their sons to the levy; a pasha governs Ottoman Hungary from Buda; Crimean Tatar raids sell Polish and Russian captives at Caffa.

> **Further in.** The Topkapı Palace keeps a talismanic shirt that took three years to make, because each stage had to wait for the right star.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
The Islamic world's learned magic is Hermetic too. It grew from the same root as the Children of the Emerald Tablet, and its schools are their own, not a reskin of Europe's.

- **The science of letters** (*ʿilm al-ḥurūf*) works through the numerical values of the Arabic letters, the names of God and magic squares. Its classic grimoire, the *Shams al-maʿārif* attributed to al-Būnī, took its best-known form in this century. Jurists condemn it as sorcery; Sufi and scholarly circles copy it widely.
- **Talismans.** Rulers wear shirts of Qurʾanic text, divine names, magic squares and star signs under their armor; ordinary people wear folded paper amulets from a *hoca* or *fqih* against the jinn and the evil eye.
- **Healing.** Qurʾanic recitation, amulets and the *baraka* of saints' tombs, where the possessed are brought, beside hospitals centuries old (al-Mansuri in Cairo, al-Nuri in Damascus, Istanbul's *darüşşifa*s). Cairo and Istanbul find Lanternhall's fame puzzling.
- **Holy warriors.** Islam's ghazis do the sworn holy work like any Paladin (see Magic, Faith and Wisdom), on the Danube and at Candia as on the Swahili coast.
- **The preachers.** The Kadızadeli preachers condemn shrine visits, saint veneration, Sufi music and dance, coffee, tobacco and Ibn ʿArabī as illicit innovation, and in 1666 Mehmed IV banned the Mevlevi whirling and the Halveti *dhikr*. The whirling is a working, a remembrance that opens the dervish to God, so the ban took magic off Istanbul's streets as well as music. The lodges still turn, behind closed doors (see Powers and Factions, The Brotherhoods of the Road).

> *"They closed the lodge, so we turn in the cellar. The preacher says it's innovation. The sick man we turned for walked home."* (a Mevlevi dervish in Istanbul)

> **Further in.** The Qurʾan says Solomon commanded the jinn, who built for him. Europe's Solomonic conjurers take their name from the same king.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
The jinn are what Islam says they are: a moral people of smokeless fire who marry, die and will be judged, some of them believers, and not part of the Hidden (see The Plenum, The Hidden Realm). They live in ruins, wells, bathhouses, drains and thresholds and punish harm done to them even by accident, so people say *bismillāh* (in Turkish, *destur*, "by your leave") before pouring hot water. Calling them fairies or monsters can give offense.

What the Hidden are in these lands is mostly open. The record here is scripture and 19th- and 20th-century ethnography, and the village edge fits badly: the jinn live inside the threshold, and the Bedouin and Yörük have no edge at all.

- **The pari**, the Turkish peri in green cloud-garments, are Persia's, and are described there (see Safavid Persia).
- **The ghul** haunts the desert, takes any shape but keeps its ass's hooves and calls travelers by name. One blow kills it; a second revives it. Whether it is a pari is open.
- **The Āl,** the *albastı*, attacks mothers and newborns, and iron under the pillow guards against it (unverified): the nearest thing here to Europe's stolen children.
- **Not the Hidden:** the div of the *Shahnameh*, an ogre that keeps its soul outside its body; the *majdhūb*, "one drawn," seized by God and revered as a saint; and Khiḍr, the Green One, who meets travelers and vanishes. Zar possession isn't recorded until 1839.

> **Further in.** In Morocco the healing brotherhood of the Hamadsha seeks out ʿAisha Qandisha, a hoofed spirit-woman who lives by the water. How early her cult is attested is unclear.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **Candia.** The siege of Venetian Crete, begun in 1648, enters what in our history is its last full year (see Central and Eastern Europe).
- **The Mevlevi ban** is two years old, and the preachers are pressing.
- **Sabbatai Zevi,** the claimed Jewish messiah, converted to Islam before the sultan in 1666.
- **Persia** crowns its shah a second time, at a better hour (see Safavid Persia).
- **Morocco.** Al-Rashīd annexes the Dilāʾ and moves about 1,300 Jewish families from there to Fez.
- **Evliya Çelebi** is on the road through Greece, Crimea and Rumelia, recording shrines.
- **Mutapa** is a customer and a careful partner. Its trade runs through Muslim hands from the Swahili coast to Gujarat, and the Porte would rather tax that trade than fight over it. Istanbul still matters, but now there's Sofala.

> **Further in.** The chief astrologer has had a Mutapan device taken apart on his table.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **Candia's end.** In our history the city surrenders in September 1669, and every power with a man inside wants something out first.
- **The preachers' reach.** The ban stopped the street rites; the next step is the observatory and the talisman-makers, and the Köprülü have to decide whether the preachers are useful.
- **The captives.** Algiers holds tens of thousands of Christian captives; Malta and Livorno hold Muslim galley slaves. Ransom brokers work both sides.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The citadel.** A Venetian commander and a grand vizier each want something in Candia's citadel that neither will name, and the party is hired by both.
- **The broken astrolabe.** A Kadızadeli follower has smashed a talisman-maker's instruments in Istanbul; the talisman-maker wants the shirt he was making finished on time, and its stars won't wait.
- **The ransom.** A broker carries a Livorno merchant's ransom to Algiers, and the taifa has just sold the captive on.
- **The renegade.** A corsair captain from Haarlem took a Mutapan device off a Portuguese prize and wants a buyer before the dey hears of it.

sections.heading: Playing Here
sections.text:
A party here works for the Porte at Candia, a lodge the preachers want closed, a ransom broker in Algiers or a European embassy that needs a dragoman.

- **Natural fits:** a **Wizard** of the science of letters; a **Natural Philosopher** in Taqi al-Din's line, or a **Counsellor** who picks the hours at court (*The Classes*); a **Physician** of the darüşşifa, unimpressed by Lanternhall; a **Paladin** of the ghazis or a **Cleric** of the mosque; a dervish **Monk** of a banned lodge; a *deli* scout as a **Barbarian**, in leopard skin and eagle feathers; a janissary **Fighter**, levied as a boy and paid late ever since; a corsair captain as a **Counsellor** Factor in all but name.
- **Backgrounds:** **Schooled** (a madrasa), **Court Creature**, **Veteran of the German Wars** (from the other side of the Danube) and **Buccaneer** (a corsair of the taifa).
- **Good outsiders:** a Venetian dragoman, a Morisco of Salé who still speaks Spanish at home, a Mutapan envoy at the Porte.
- **The law.** No license: sharia courts judge sorcery, the chief astrologer answers for learned magic at court and the preachers decide what the street will tolerate.
- **The question every character here answers:** is what you do piety or innovation, and who gets to say?

sections.heading: Open for Developers
sections.text:
- **The Islamic lands' Hidden beside the jinn.** Their names and faces from the Maghreb to the Gulf where the jinn are not (the pari, the ghul, the spirits of wells and ruins), written from the record and with care; who keeps the villages; and how the Wild Hunt rides here in the dark half. Persia's pari are the anchor (see Safavid Persia).
- **The ghazi orders' name.** The setting's name for Islam's sworn holy warriors, and how their oaths differ from the Knights of Malta's.
- **The Porte and Mutapa.** Whether Istanbul is on the same alert as the European courts, and what the chief astrologer read in the parts on his table.
- **Morocco under al-Rashīd.** A new dynasty, a conquered Sufi state and a sultan who will want Timbuktu (see West Africa).

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
Safavid Persia is a large, settled empire at peace with all its neighbors, and in 1668 it is watching the sky. Isfahan is among the largest cities in the world, and its Armenian suburb runs a trading network from Amsterdam to Manila. After a year of famine and a great earthquake, the court decided the shah had been crowned at the wrong hour, and on Nowruz 1668 it crowned him again under a new name.

**The one thing to remember:** in Persia the people who read the stars hold real power, and the people who read the Law are rising to take it from them. The hour is a matter of state, and an hour can be chosen again.

> **Further in.** Follow the silk: west with New Julfa's Armenians to Venice and Amsterdam, or by Aleppo and Smyrna (see The Ottomans and the Islamic West); south through Bandar Abbas onto the Monsoon Road (see The Indian Ocean); east by Kandahar to the Mughals (see Mughal India).

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
A high plateau ringed by mountains, with salt desert at its heart and every town placed where water can be brought to it.

- **The qanats.** Tunnels carry groundwater by gravity for miles out of the mountains to the oasis towns. A town ends where its water does.
- **The Caspian shore.** Gilan and Mazandaran are wet, forested rice and silk country, and crown land; Abbas I's palace town, **Farahabad**, is here.
- **Hard years.** Drought, locusts and famine in 1666–67 brought food riots, and in November 1667 an earthquake in Shirvan killed over 30,000 in its villages and about 20,000 in Shamakhi, the silk town.

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The shah.** Solayman, about 21, was crowned as Safi II in October 1666 and again in March 1668. Raised in the harem, he drinks heavily, governs more and more from the harem and will never lead an army.
- **The inner council.** His mother, a Circassian named Nakihat Khanom, and three senior eunuchs, Agha Kafur, Agha Mobarak and Agha Kamal, decide what reaches him.
- **The grand vizier.** Mirza Mohammad Karaki runs the administration outside the harem. In our history he falls in 1669 to Shaykh Ali Khan Zanganeh.
- **The clergy.** Sabzavari, *shaykh al-islam* of Isfahan, presided over both coronations. Behind him rises Majlesi, about 40. The clergy are a confident establishment, beginning to push the shah.
- **The army.** The *qizilbash*, the Turkmen cavalry who won the dynasty its throne, are shrinking; the **ghulams**, Georgian, Armenian and Circassian captives and converts, serve as cavalry, officials and governors.
- **New Julfa.** About 30,000 Armenians, deported here in 1604–05, elect their own mayor, ship the empire's silk and pay the queen mother's stipend in taxes.
- **The edges.** Tabriz watches the Ottoman frontier and Herat the Uzbeks; at Bandar Abbas the Dutch factory has outweighed the English since 1645; Kandahar has held against the Mughals' heaviest guns since 1649.
- **The conquered.** Jews were forcibly converted twice, most recently in 1656–62. Zoroastrians in Yazd and Kerman are squeezed for taxes and labor by Isfahan's officials and the province's alike.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Here the hour is a working, and the men who choose it sit near the throne (see Powers and Factions, Institutions Beyond Europe).

- **The chief astrologer** casts the *ekhtiyarat*, the "elections": the propitious moment for an audience, a journey, a campaign, a building or a coronation, read mainly from the moon. He presents the year's almanac at Nowruz and stands near the shah with an astrolabe (unverified).
- **The election works.** An act begun at an elected hour carries that hour's stars to its end. A good hour doesn't win a battle; a bad one sours everything that follows, until someone begins the thing again.
- **The wrong hour.** When famine and the earthquake followed the first coronation, the physicians blamed the astrologers' date, and the queen mother, the chief physician and the chief eunuchs ordered a second ceremony.
- **The substitute king.** Tavernier tells of a Zoroastrian set on the throne first, then replaced by a statue that was beheaded, so the bad stars would fall elsewhere. Here it worked, and the man who carried the shah's stars off the throne is still somewhere in Isfahan.
- **The clergy's days.** Theologians condemn astrology as denying God's power, and Shiʿi scholars keep their own lists of lucky and unlucky days from the Imams' sayings; Majlesi is credited with one (unverified). The clergy's days against the astrologers' hours is the quarrel of the age.
- **The Sufis.** The dynasty began as a Sufi order and the shah is still nominally its "perfect guide," but the polemics against Sufis are multiplying. Sufi remembrance is a real working here as in Istanbul's lodges, so the campaign is against a magic as much as a doctrine.
- **Every faith's holy work answers,** a rabbi's in Kashan as surely as a jurist's in Isfahan.

**At the table.** A court astrologer (an NPC of the trade, hired or owed a favor) can spend 10 minutes electing the hour for one venture, once per Long Rest; a venture is a journey, a battle or a negotiation the DM agrees is one undertaking. When the venture begins at that hour, one creature of the astrologer's choice who takes part gains Heroic Inspiration. The Court Astrologer's Astrolabe (Characters) finds the day's auspicious hour, a separate benefit; neither needs the other.

> **Further in.** In 1722 the last Safavid shah delayed battle on his astrologers' advice, fed his troops a broth to make them invisible and lost Isfahan.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
**A note on the name.** In Twelver Shiʿism the Twelfth Imam is the Hidden Imam, in occultation since 874. He is a holy figure of a living faith and has nothing to do with the setting's Hidden; this chapter calls the Hidden here by their own name, the pari.

- **The pari.** The jinn are not part of the Hidden (see The Ottomans and the Islamic West). The pari, whose homeland this is, behave in the game as Hidden; the learned count them among the jinn, and the book doesn't call that wrong. Supremely beautiful and morally mixed, they carry people off to **Paristan**, sometimes to a pari wedding, in body or in trance, and make love matches with humans that end when a taboo is broken. They are one people from Isfahan to Delhi to the Kazakh steppe (see Mughal India and The Steppe and the North). The cover's Persian elf is a pari.
- **The Āl,** the childbed spirit of Iran, Armenia and the Caucasus, is a thin old woman with a clay nose who carries off a new mother's liver; in Armenian lore she steals a baby within forty days of birth. Iron, onions, garlic and prayer guard the forty days. The tradition calls her a demon; she is a low pari that took a demon's name. (unverified: her Persian record before the 19th century)
- **Not the pari:** the Twelve Imams; Khidr, the Green One; the Zoroastrian yazatas, Ahriman and the fravashis; the divs of the *Shahnameh*; and the **Simurgh**, nearer the divine.
- **The edge** fits the oasis towns: past the last garden is the waste. The Zagros herders have none. Persians reckon Paristan nearest at Nowruz, and the Wild Hunt rides through the northern dark half (see Running Euphonia, Running the Hidden).

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The second coronation.** On Nowruz, 20 March, at nine in the morning in the Chehel Sotun, Safi II is crowned again as **Solayman**. A comet follows; the sources disagree whether the astrologers read it as portent or good omen.
- **Razin on the Caspian.** Stenka Razin's Cossacks fail at Derbent, raid toward Baku, lose about 400 men at Rasht and send envoys to Isfahan asking for land. Then they pose as merchants in **Farahabad** and sack it.
- **Basra.** The Ottomans take Basra, on the Gulf border, back into direct rule.
- **The witnesses.** Chardin saw both coronations and will publish them in Paris in 1671.
- **The Book of the Forced Converts.** In Kashan, Babai ben Lotf is setting down his community's forced conversions in Persian verse in Hebrew letters.

> **Further in.** In our history Razin's Cossacks destroy a Persian fleet off Pig Island in July 1669. The tale that he drowned a Persian princess in the Volga comes from a Dutch sailor, and historians doubt it.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The new hour.** One side at court needs it to hold; another needs it to fail, and the next disaster will be read as a verdict.
- **The rising cleric.** Majlesi is compiling a vast hadith collection and putting doctrine into plain Persian. In our history he girds the next shah himself in 1694, in place of the Sufi who always had, and the coffeehouses close.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The forty days.** A Georgian ghulam's wife has given birth. The midwives have their iron and onions, but something has already carried her liver toward the river.
- **The substitute.** A man who sat on the throne for a few minutes is walking around Isfahan with a shah's bad stars, and someone wants them back on the shah.
- **The eunuchs' gate.** A petition, a warning or a Mutapan gift has to reach the shah, and it has to get past Agha Kafur, Agha Mobarak and Agha Kamal first.
- **The pari wedding.** A New Julfa merchant's son went to one at Nowruz and hasn't come back, and his family's letters reach from Amsterdam to Manila.

sections.heading: Playing Here
sections.text:
A party here works for a faction at court, a New Julfa house, a governor or a foreign factory that wants to know what the stars have said.

- **Natural fits:** a **Wizard** who is a court astrologer, with an almanac and an enemy among the physicians; a **Physician** in the chief physician's circle who blames the stars for nothing, or a **Natural Philosopher** from Mashhad's astrolabe workshops (*The Classes*); a Sufi **Monk** in a lodge the clergy want closed; a ghulam **Paladin**, sworn to the shah who owns him; a **Cleric** who is a Shiʿi jurist, an Armenian priest or a Zoroastrian priest of Yazd; a **Bard**, a *naqqal* telling the *Shahnameh* with a stick for a sword (unverified: coffeehouse recitation in this reign); a **Counsellor** Factor for New Julfa or Spymaster for the eunuchs; a **Hidden Killer** who guards the forty days, or a **Warlock** of the Dreamlord back from a pari wedding (*Life on the Border*).
- **Backgrounds:** **Schooled**, **Court Creature** and **Company Factor**.
- **Good outsiders:** a Capuchin interpreter (Raphaël du Mans has held the post since about 1650), a Dutch or English factor, a Georgian prince at court, a Cossack "merchant," a Mutapan envoy with a lamp the astrologers want to read.
- **The law.** Nobody issues a license. The chief astrologer serves the court, the clergy judge what is lawful and a practitioner's safety is whichever of them is winning.
- **The question every character here answers:** who chooses the hour, and what will you do if they chose wrong?

sections.heading: Open for Developers
sections.text:
- **The chief astrologer of 1668.** A name and a person for the office, and his rivals among the physicians.
- **The perfect guide.** Whether the shah's title as head of the Safavid order still does anything, and what a Sufi lodge can ask of him.
- **Carrying the stars.** What happens to a substitute who takes a ruler's ill hour, written as flavor first; anything with a rule is simmed first.
- **The pari's realm.** Paristan, the pari's own names and ranks, who now holds the keys to the cages where the *Shahnameh*'s divs kept them, and whether the ghul are pari.
- **The Khorasan frontier in the dark half.** What the Wild Hunt looks like where Uzbek and Turkmen raiders also ride, and how a village tells which came.

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
West Africa in 1668 is a crowded field of strong states: Muslim cavalry kingdoms in the Sahel, the Yoruba kingdoms and their holy city, gold states in the Akan forest, a sacred king at Benin and slave-trading kingdoms on the lagoons.

**The one thing to remember:** the Europeans are tenants. Every fort stands on ground an African ruler rents out, and what the coast sells is decided ashore. In 1668 it sells gold, and more and more it sells people.

> **Further in.** The caravans go north to Morocco (see The Ottomans and the Islamic West); the ships go west to Brazil and Barbados (see South America), north to Amsterdam and London (see Western Europe) or south to Luanda (see West-Central Africa).

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
The bands run east to west: desert edge, savanna, forest, coast.

- **The Sahel and the savanna.** Camel country with the desert ports of Timbuktu, Gao and Agadez; south of it millet, cattle and horses, the cavalry states' country.
- **The forest.** Farmed, tapped and full of towns and shrines: Benin, Ijebu, Ilesa and the Akan kingdoms. The **Dahomey Gap**, where savanna reaches the sea west of Allada, is the one road a horse can take to the coast.
- **The tsetse line.** The fly kills horses, so cavalry can raid the forest but can't live in it. Oyo can't breed enough horses and buys them from Nupe and Borgu, the neighbors it fights.
- **The coast.** Lagoons and mangrove creeks east of the Volta; surf on the gold shore, where canoemen ferry every cargo out to the ships. Europeans call the shores the Gold Coast and the Slave Coast: the cargo, not the people.
- **The harmattan**, the dusty wind off the Sahara, blows roughly November to March: the caravan and campaign season.
- **Fever** kills newcomers on the coast at very high rates. No European army operates inland anywhere here.

> *"The Dutchman asks where the gold comes from. I tell him: from upriver. He builds a fort upriver. We burn it. Then he asks again."* (an Akan broker at Elmina)

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
**The Yoruba world** is a family of kingdoms with one language, one holy city and one sacred line of kings, not one empire.

- **Ile-Ife** is the homeland. Its king, the **Ooni**, descends from Oduduwa, as every crowned Yoruba king claims to.
- **Oyo** is the rising power, home from decades of exile after the Nupe took its capital. Abipa brought the court back around 1610.
- **The Alaafin isn't absolute.** The seven councilors of the **Oyo Mesi**, led by the **Basorun**, choose him and can order him to take his own life. The Alaafin in 1668 is **Ajagbo** (unverified). **The Ogboni**, the elders' society tied to the Earth, judge bloodshed and mediate between council and king.
- **The others** (Ijebu, Ilesa, Owo, Ketu, the Egba towns) are independent and often hostile; Ilesa's forest fought Oyo's cavalry to a standstill. Oyo forbids enslaving its own subjects, and in 1668 taxes the trade more than it feeds it.

**The lagoons.** **Allada** controls the ports of Offra and Whydah, pays tribute to Oyo and is the great slave-selling kingdom of its coast, about 125,000 people between 1640 and 1690; its king is **Tezifon** (unverified). Inland, **Dahomey** is small, under its first king.

**The forest kings.**

- **Benin's oba** no longer leads armies: he is a sacred king secluded in a palace in Benin City hung with brass plaques, and his chiefs are taking the power he doesn't use. The record doesn't settle who reigns in the 1660s, so this book names no oba (unverified).
- **Denkyira** is the great Akan power under **Boa Amponsem I**, with a treasury called the *Sikadan*, "house of gold"; the future Asante are among its tributaries. **Akwamu**, behind Accra, is a rising military state with musketeers and hereditary slave-soldiers.

**The savanna and the Sahel.**

- **Bornu**'s **Mai Ali** came home from his third pilgrimage to Mecca in 1667 to a revolt.
- **Kano and Katsina** made peace to face the **Kwararafa** of the Benue, who broke into Kano in 1653.
- **The Arma**, heirs of the Moroccan army that broke Songhay in 1591, rule Timbuktu and the Niger bend from river forts and stopped answering to Morocco in 1660. Their pashas rarely last a year.
- **Senegambia.** The Wolof kingdoms' warrior aristocracies, the *ceddo*, and **Kaabu**, a Mandinka federation, fund their wars by selling captives.

**The tenants.** The **Dutch West India Company** is strongest, from **Elmina**, taken from Portugal in 1637. **The English** Royal Adventurers hold **Cape Coast Castle** and **James Island** in the Gambia, and brand their captives "DoY," for the Duke of York (see Powers and Factions, The Chartered Companies). **The Danes** hold **Christiansborg**, bought from Great Accra's king; **the French** have Saint-Louis on the Senegal.

> **Further in.** In 1665 the Dutch stormed the English fort at Kormantin with about 1,200 African allies, while the English had African allies of their own. African armies decide which company keeps its forts.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Every tradition here is a Wisdom tradition or a learned one, and most are both (see Magic, Faith and Wisdom).

- **The Yoruba are West Africa's Andes:** the Indigenous power whose Wisdom tradition makes it a match for anyone. It belongs to the Yoruba as a people, not to one kingdom, and Ifá's priests serve them all. In the field it looks like **spirit riding**, the orisha mounting their devotees: when Oyo's cavalry rides, some of its riders are ridden.
- **Ifá** is learned Wisdom. A *babaláwo*, "father of secrets," casts palm nuts or a divination chain to find one of 256 *odu*, chants its verses and prescribes sacrifice. Kings consult it before every great decision: a priesthood that studies like scholars.
- **The orisha** answer their priests. Shango, remembered as a king of Oyo, is thunder, and lightning-struck stones are kept at his shrines; Ogun clears roads and works iron; Eshu carries offerings between the worlds and is not the Devil.
- **The Ogboni's brass staffs**, cast in pairs and joined by a chain, are held to be the Earth's vessel, not its picture. An oath sworn on them binds.
- **Benin's oba** has his power renewed each year in the Igue rite, and his *obo* cure and counter witches; the Akan *okomfo* is a priest-medium possessed by a god after years of training.
- **Vodun.** Allada and Whydah have their own gods, and Whydah keeps a royal python. The well-known Dahomean pantheon is built after 1668.
- **Islam's learning.** Timbuktu's family libraries survived conquest; Katsina's scholars are known for mathematics and the occult sciences, the science of letters and sand-divination among them.

> **Further in.** Ifá's binary signs closely resemble Arabic sand-divination, *khatt al-raml*, and scholars disagree on how the two are related.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Nearly all of this is 19th- and 20th-century record of living belief; the 17th-century record is European traders calling everything "fetish."

- **The owners of the land.** Every forest, river and rock has owners, and an earth priest bargains with them: the Mossi *tengasoba*, the Yoruba and Edo groves, the Poro forest. This is the region's village edge, and the Hidden Killers watch it. West Africa keeps the northern calendar, so the Hunt's raiding season falls in the harmattan, when the caravans and the armies are on the road too.
- **The bori** (Hausa), spirits of families, places, animals and rocks sorted into twelve "houses," are handled by a possession cult, mostly women, led in some kingdoms by a chief priestess, the **Inna**. Muslim Hausa call them *aljannu*, jinn; in the game they behave as Hidden, as the pari do (see Safavid Persia), and the book doesn't call the Hausa wrong.
- **The teachers.** The Fon **aziza** of anthills and silk-cotton trees give hunters good magic; the Akan **mmoatia**, forest folk about a foot high with backward feet, teach herbs to priests (unverified); whoever takes a Yoruba **egbere**'s little mat grows rich. Here the Hidden teach professions.
- **The abiku** (Yoruba; the Igbo *ogbanje*) are children who belong to a company in the spirit world and die to go back to it unless rites hold them. The belief is bound up with real child deaths and real grief; handle it with weight.
- **Not the Hidden:** Benin's Olokun and the Yoruba river orisha, who are gods. Water spirits of wealth and seduction are old here, but the name Mami Wata isn't recorded until 1775.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The trade is growing.** Nearly half a million people were shipped from all of Africa in 1651–75, and the number is rising; the desert trade still takes about 7,000 a year north. **Who resists:** Muslim scholars who refuse to sell Muslims to Christians, Benin, which restricts the sale of men (unverified), and the people who run.
- **Dapper's book**, out in Amsterdam this year, shows Europe Benin's brass palace (see West-Central Africa).
- **Oyo** holds its northern line against Nupe and Borgu and looks southwest, toward Allada.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The Kwararafa.** In our history they break Kano again in 1671, and a Katsina scholar's prayers are credited with killing their commander.
- **The penitents.** A Saharan preacher north of the Senegal calls for repentance and an end to slave raiding; in our history his movement topples four kingdoms in 1673.
- **Morocco's new sultan will want Timbuktu back,** and the Arma don't agree on an answer (see The Ottomans and the Islamic West).

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The horse.** Oyo's master of horse wants a druid or healer who can keep a horse alive past the tsetse line, and every kingdom south of it wants that person gone.
- **Akwamu and Great Accra.** A rising army, a rich neighbor and a Danish castle whose landlord may change; the Danes want to know which way to lean.
- **The mat.** A trader at Ijebu market is suddenly, inexplicably rich, and the egbere who lost the mat wants it back.
- **The roads at Offra.** A company ship is loading captives, and a family ashore has come to buy one of them back before it sails.

sections.heading: Playing Here
sections.text:
A party here works for a king who rents out a fort, a company that rents one, a desert caravan house or a family trying to get someone back.

- **Natural fits:** a **Cleric** of an orisha, or a babaláwo as a **Cleric** or **Druid**; a **Wizard** of the science of letters from Katsina's schools or Timbuktu's; a **Fighter** of Oyo's cavalry or an Akwamu musketeer; an Akan **Revelator** taught by the mmoatia; a **Counsellor** Factor for a company or for the king who rents it a fort (*The Classes*); a griot as a **Bard**, a court's memory and its envoy; a **Hidden Killer** walking the owners' land (*Life on the Border*).
- **Backgrounds:** **Company Factor**, **Schooled** (a Timbuktu family library) and **Border-Born**.
- **Good outsiders:** a Portuguese-African trader from the Gambia, a Danish soldier at Christiansborg, a Moroccan envoy to the Arma, a Capuchin who learned Allada's language.
- **The law.** Each king's: a fort's company answers to the ruler who rents it the ground, and the priests and societies judge magic in their own courts.
- **The question every character here answers:** who are you selling to, and who are you selling?

sections.heading: Open for Developers
sections.text:
- **Where the Yoruba power gathers:** at Ife, the holy city, at Oyo, the empire, or both; and what spirit riding looks like in a cavalry charge.
- **Ifá at the table.** Ifá as Wisdom with Intelligence's structure, written by someone who knows it.
- **What the Hidden take for the lesson.** The aziza, mmoatia and egbere teach luck, medicine and wealth; the price, and whether the mmoatia's healers are the taken who came back.
- **The Hunt in the harmattan,** and where the iroko's spirit and Sasabonsam stand: among the Hidden or outside them.

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
West-Central Africa is a Christian kingdom with its crown in pieces. Kongo has been Catholic for 150 years, with its own nobles, schools and books in Kikongo, and in 1665, at Mbwila, an army from Portuguese Luanda killed its king and much of its nobility. Two royal houses now fight over the throne. The power rising out of the wreck is **Soyo**, Kongo's own coastal province at the mouth of the Congo, rich on salt and Dutch trade, which has beaten every army sent against it.

**The one thing to remember:** the question in 1668 is whether Soyo reunites Kongo before Portugal, Matamba or the civil war decides it.

> **Further in.** This is the busiest slaving coast in the Atlantic, and nearly everyone here is part of it, Soyo included. Its ships go to Brazil (see South America), its governors come from there and its trophies go to Lisbon (see Western Europe).

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
- **The river that swallows rivers.** The Congo (*Nzadi*) pours out more water than any river but the Amazon. Soyo holds its south bank and the old port of Mpinda.
- **The falls.** Above the estuary the river drops through some 32 falls and rapids over about 220 miles. No ship passes; everything beyond, from the Tio markets at Malebo Pool inward, is reached on foot or by canoe.
- **The Kwanza** is Portugal's road inland; **the Kwango** to the east is the edge of the Atlantic's reach, where Kasanje holds the farthest market.
- **The country.** Savanna and wooded hills, forest along the rivers and in the Mayombe, drier toward the Namib. One long rainy season, roughly October to May, and a cool dry season, the *cacimbo* (unverified).
- **The fever coast.** Newcomers from Europe die at catastrophic rates, and horses rarely survive, probably for the tsetse (unverified). Portugal's armies here are mostly African, led by a few hundred musketeers, many of them convicts from Brazil. Smallpox is the worst of the epidemics.
- **Money is cloth and shells:** raffia squares, and the *nzimbu* shells of Luanda island, the Kongo king's money until Portugal took the island around 1650.

> *"In São Salvador they pay the teacher in shells. In Luanda they pay the soldier in cloth. Nobody pays anyone in Portuguese coin, including the Portuguese."* (a Vili trader at Mpinda)

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The king at São Salvador.** Álvaro VIII, of the Kinlaza house, holds the capital because Soyo put him there in 1666. He ceded mining rights in Mbamba and Mpemba to Portugal in 1667, which his nobles haven't forgiven.
- **The houses.** The **Kinlaza** and the **Kimpanzu** (*kanda*, royal lineages) each claim the throne. A Kimpanzu rival, Afonso II, holds out at Nkondo in the east; a Kinlaza rival, Pedro III, is already counting Álvaro's guards.
- **The electors.** Kongo's king is chosen by senior officeholders, one of them the ruler of Soyo. The European titles (duke, marquis, count) were put on Kongo offices in the 1500s and stand for the rank.
- **Soyo.** Count **Paulo da Silva** rules the richest province in Kongo: the only one with a port and salt, a capital of about 30,000 and a fortified sacred wood, **Nfinda Ngula**, that no army has taken. Soyo threw back four royal invasions (1641–1656) and sent its own ambassador to Dutch Brazil, and its rulers call themselves princes now. **The Dutch** trade at Mpinda and sell Soyo guns and powder; they build no forts here.
- **Portuguese Angola.** Luanda, Benguela and a string of river forts reaching about 190 miles inland, run by a junta since February 1667. Its money, ships and last governors came from Brazil.
- **Matamba.** Queen Njinga died in 1663 and her sister Barbara in 1666. Barbara's husband, Njinga a Mona, an Imbangala-trained commander, has seized power; João Guterres, the man the Church wouldn't let Barbara marry, wants it.
- **Kasanje,** a war-state on the Kwango founded by the Imbangala, a society built by initiation instead of kinship. Its king, **Pascoal**, strangled his adoptive father for the throne, was baptized two years later and sells captives to Luanda as its "general."
- **Loango**, north of the river, has a Christian king and **Vili** merchants carrying copper and cloth to Malebo Pool.
- **The conquered.** Every power here sells captives; the civil war has made the trade bigger and Soyo richer.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
Kongo's church named its priests with the word for its healers. When the Jesuits and Kongolese teachers put the faith into Kikongo, "holy" became *nkisi*, the word for a spirit-charged object; a priest became an *nganga*; a church became *nzo a ukisi*, the house of holiness. The setting's rule that holiness works for whoever is holy (see Magic, Faith and Wisdom) was already written into Kongo's vocabulary.

- **The church is Kongolese.** It runs on noble lay teachers, the *mestres*, paid in shells, on brotherhoods, on Kongo's own Order of Christ and on a Jesuit college in São Salvador. Since 1624 the bishop has lived in Luanda and ordains no Kongolese, so a village's holy work is done by whoever is holy, and a mestre casts as a Cleric with no ordination at all.
