- **A vertical country.** A ladder of climates: fog desert, coca and maize valleys, potato slopes, *puna* grassland above 13,500 feet, and ice. Communities hold land at several heights at once, tied by kin and ritual: an "archipelago" of floors.
- **Terraces and frost.** Terraces hold soil, carry water and make their own microclimates. Above about 12,500 feet families freeze-dry potatoes into *chuño* that keeps for years, and the high ground can outlast a siege on it.
- **Potosí.** About 13,000 feet up under Cerro Rico, with some 120,000 people. Nothing grows there: food, fuel and timber come in on llama trains, the mills run on dammed glacial lakes and contraband silver leaks out to Buenos Aires.
- **Huancavelica.** Potosí's mercury comes from "the mine of death," some 600 miles away.
- **The coast.** One of the driest places on earth, with the guano islands offshore; every few years El Niño kills the fishery.
- **The Chocó.** Pacific rainforest with 33 to 43 feet of rain a year at some gauges. The rivers are the only roads: the Atrato north to the Caribbean, the San Juan south to the Pacific. Every gravel bar holds gold, and with it grains of a "little silver" that won't pan out. Malarial, and lethal to outsiders.
- **The Amazon's edge.** The Inca's Antisuyu, traded with and never mastered; much of the forest is managed land, and in 1639 the Portuguese counted over 400 Omagua villages on the middle river.

> *"Down on the coast they wait for the ship. Up there they eat potatoes they froze before you were born. Guess who wins a long war."* (a muleteer on the Potosí road)

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The Sapa Inca.** The son of the Sun, here literally: Inti's son by blood, he shows it by power, and the succession goes to whichever royal son the Sun answers. He rules from Cuzco again by bargaining with the huacas, which now answer back.
- **The huacas.** Sacred beings with a material presence: mountains, springs, stones, oracles and the mummified dead, who are dressed, fed and consulted. They compete, marry and quarrel; the *apus*, the mountain lords, rank by height. The Inca have always negotiated with them, and punished them.
- **The kurakas and the conquered.** Local lords kept their posts under Spain and sit on both sides of the line. Tawantinsuyu was built on conquest: the Cañari and Chachapoya fought beside Spain, and by one estimate nearly half the old empire treated the Spanish as liberators.
- **Spain.** A viceroy in Lima rules with the Church, and the Archbishop of Lima's campaign against "idolatry" is at its height (1646–1670). In our history Potosí ran on the *mita*, a forced labor draft. Here it never came: Potosí runs on paid workers and the old Inca rotation, the *mit'a*, on Inca terms.
- **The Mapuche.** Independent by treaty since the Parliament of Quilín in 1641. Spain's Chilean frontier, south of Santiago, is an army post paid for from Peru.
- **Portugal's Brazil**, governed from Salvador. Sugar mills worked by enslaved Africans, and *bandeirantes* raiding inland for captives.
- **Palmares.** A *quilombo* in the hills of Pernambuco since about 1605: fortified towns of 11,000 to 20,000 escaped Africans, Indigenous people and poor Portuguese, with an elected king.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
The Andes are the strongest Indigenous power in the Americas: Wisdom magic and the world's best high-altitude engineering, working together (Magic, Faith and Wisdom).

- **Engineering.** Roads of 19,000 to 25,000 miles with relay runners, fiber suspension bridges, earthquake-proof walls and the *khipu*, knotted-cord records (Characters has the Khipu of Record).
- **Weather and flood are weapons.** Manco Inca flooded the plain at Ollantaytambo. Lightning has its own priests: whoever survives a strike, a priest recorded in 1621, "is as though divinely chosen for the ministry of the huacas."
- **The huacas rose.** During Taki Onqoy (c. 1564–72) followers said the huacas had left the stones and lakes to enter human bodies, and the possessed were painted red and worshipped. Here they rose. Keepers speak for them: for each huaca, for the mummies, for lightning, for the sun.
- **Medicine.** Cinchona bark from Loja cures malaria; Jesuits learned it from local people, and Protestant England calls it "Popish powder." The Kallawaya healers of the Bolivian highlands carry a pharmacopoeia of about 980 plants.
- **Platina.** Spain finds platinum grains mixed with Chocó gold, can't separate them, stores them and throws them back into the rivers under a notary's certificate so no one can fake gold with them. The only known pre-Hispanic platinum work, on the La Tolita–Tumaco coast, sintered the grains with gold below the melting point. How the powers found out is in Adventures and Hooks, The Great Game.
- **The jaibaná.** Emberá and Wounaan specialists of the Chocó, men and women, who capture *jai*, the animating force of everything and of disease, keep a carved staff for each illness and die if an enemy destroys the staff. They're hired to "open" a river for settlement. The 17th-century record says shamans were the main resistance to Spain; the detail is 20th-century ethnography.
- **The *machi*** (Mapuche). Called by dreams or an illness, climbs a notched tree in trance and drums on the *kultrun*; a *kalku*, a sorcerer, is a machi the spirits overcame. In 1668 a machi is as likely to be a man, or of mixed gender, as a woman.

> **Further in.** Mutapa's platinum has its ultimate use in nitric acid, which means fertilizer. The Inca have rationed guano by province for centuries, and Spain doesn't value it.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
The huacas are closer to gods than to Hidden folk: the pantheon that rose. The Hidden are something else, recorded by priests out to destroy them in the Andes and by 19th- and 20th-century writers in the lowlands.

- **The people of the old age** (Andes). The *machu* or "gentiles" lived before the present sun and were dried to bones when it rose. They haunt old tombs and ruins by night and cause wasting illness. The name *machu* is recorded later (unverified); the 1621 record has an earlier form, ancestors in caves who sicken those who neglect them.
- **The owners of places** (Chocó). The Emberá *wãndra*, "jealous and surly," live at headwaters and waterfalls and can take jaguar form. Pãkðré, the mother-in-law of the animals, kidnaps hunters.
- **The curupira** (Tupi coast). The best-dated Hidden figure on the continent: in 1560 a Jesuit recorded people leaving feathers and arrows on a mountain to placate it. It punishes over-hunting, and later accounts give it backward feet.
- **The encantados** (Amazon). The river dolphin comes to the dance in a white suit, his hat hiding his blowhole, and takes lovers down to a city under the river: the closest match to the fairy-taken, recorded only from the 19th century.
- **The fat-stealer.** In the 1570s Andeans said Spaniards were cutting people open for their fat. The *pishtaco* is the fairy turned inside out: here the dangerous stranger is the European.
- **The edge** runs up and down a mountain, because an Andean community's land is a set of floors at different heights.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The siege line** runs through Potosí. Spain holds the city; the Inca hold the mountain's approaches and Huancavelica's mercury, so every ounce of silver Spain refines is on Inca sufferance.
- **The platina.** Every power now knows what Spain is dumping. In our history Spain didn't meet platina until about 1690.
- **The Chocó** isn't secured. The Wounaan moved upriver from the missionaries, and mining families from Popayán push in.
- **Lima's extirpators** are burning mummies in the last and fiercest campaign, against huacas that answer.
- **Brazil.** The Dutch have been gone fourteen years and sugar is slipping. Spain has just recognized Portugal, which frees Lisbon to act.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The continental war.** If New Granada and its port at Cartagena fall easily, a fleet is all the Chocó costs, and the first navy up the Atrato takes the metal.
- **The visitations.** Extirpators are reaching villages whose huacas talk back.
- **The Chocó's miners.** Spain's mining there, in our history, ran on enslaved Africans; Palmares is a free kingdom, and Mutapa is African and rising.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The notary's barrels.** A season's stored platina waits to be thrown in the river, and three buyers want it first.
- **The mercury road.** A convoy from Huancavelica needs an escort, and both sides know Potosí stops without it.
- **Opening the river.** A mining company has hired a jaibaná to open a river, and the Wounaan have hired another to keep it shut.
- **The last payday.** A mercenary company on the siege line hasn't been paid since Lent, and the Inca have made an offer (The High Ground).

sections.heading: Playing Here
Open for Developers
sections.text:
- **The Sapa Inca's court.** His name, how a court governs magic when the Sun's son is literal, and how the huaca keepers sit in it.
- **The Wild Hunt here.** How it rides in the Andes, the Chocó and the Amazon, and who keeps watch on a mountain's floors.
- **What the mountains accept.** Andeans and friars both made offerings to Huaynaputina, which buried Arequipa in ash in 1600. Here the mountains answer; which offering they took is open.
- **The High Ground's first seasons:** a Spanish, an Inca and a mercenary start, with the Chocó as the shared second act (Adventures and Hooks lists them open).
- **Backgrounds.** A khipu keeper's apprenticeship (Characters, Backgrounds), a *bandeirante*, a Mapuche envoy.

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
Oceania is a sea of islands, and the sea is the road. Its peoples reached Hawaiʻi, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa centuries ago by navigation. Europe has a few charts, a VOC verdict that Australia is worthless and, this year, a Jesuit mission on its way to Guam. In the eastern Carolines stands Pohnpei, whose basalt city of Nan Madol, by tradition, two sorcerer brothers raised by magic. In Euphonia, they did.

**The one thing to remember:** Pohnpei shows what a society can do building with spells instead of brick, and what it risks relying on them alone.

> **Further in.** Nan Madol's basalt came from a volcanic plug on the far side of the island. Nobody has settled how it was moved.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
Pacific peoples had been burning forest, building fishponds and taro terraces and changing their islands for centuries.

- **High islands and atolls.** Volcanic high islands (Pohnpei, Tahiti) catch rain, run streams and feed dense populations. Atolls rise a few feet from the sea; their water is a thin lens of rain floating on salt water underground, and gardens are dug down to it (unverified).
- **Pohnpei.** A mountainous island, among the wettest on earth (unverified). Off its coast Nan Madol is a complex of artificial basalt islets; its first chiefly tomb stands over 25 feet high.
- **The reef.** Reefs and lagoons are the main larder; Hawaiian fishponds wall off the reef flats with sluice gates.
- **Wayfinding.** Navigators hold a star compass of 32 houses, read several swells at once and follow land birds home at dusk; lagoons tint the clouds above them green. Carolinian navigators imagine the canoe as still and the islands moving past it.
- **Weather and health.** Typhoons in the west, cyclones in the south, roughly November to April. Malaria stops at Vanuatu: Fiji, Polynesia and eastern Micronesia have none, and Australia has none of the Old World crowd diseases.
- **Aotearoa.** Forest in the wet west and the hills, grass and shrub where the first settlers burned the drier east. The moa, and the giant eagle *hōkioi* that hunted them, have been gone about two centuries. Kūmara grows in the north; greenstone comes from the South Island's West Coast.
- **Australia.** A continent of Country: every part named, sung, owned and cared for under Law, and kept open by planned burning. At Budj Bim the Gunditjmara have farmed eels in stone channels for 6,600 years.
- **New Guinea.** One of the world's first farming centers, at Kuk.

> *"You keep asking where the land is. Stop looking for it. Let it come to you."* (a navigator of Satawal to a Spanish pilot)

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **Pohnpei.** The Saudeleur dynasty ruled the whole island from Nan Madol until, by tradition about 1628, Isokelekel of Kosrae overthrew it. Since then power has been divided among chiefdoms under **Nahnmwarki** titles. Priests, the *samworo*, mediate with the gods and work helpful and harmful sorcery. The chiefs hold the titles and the priests the rites, and the stones answer neither by right.
- **Aotearoa.** Kin-based: *whānau* (families) within *hapū* (the working political and land-holding units) within *iwi*, under *rangatira* whose authority rests on descent, ability and *mana*. *Tapu* restricts persons of rank, burial grounds and certain acts; rites make things *noa*, common, again. Ngāti Tūmatakōkiri saw off Tasman's ships in 1642.
- **Tonga and its network.** The Tuʻi Tonga is a sacred paramount; executive power has passed to other lines (unverified). Two-thirds of the stone tools at its chiefly centers came from Samoa and Fiji.
- **The Society Islands.** Taputapuātea on Raʻiātea, dedicated to ʻOro, anchors an alliance of chiefs and priests. The traveling ʻarioi perform dramas that preserve tradition and mock the chiefs.
- **Hawaiʻi.** Rival paramount chiefs, a ranked society and *kapu*, sacred law whose breaking means death unless the offender reaches a place of refuge.
- **Australia.** About 250 language groups. Law is held by senior men and women, each holding different parts; authority rests with knowledge and age, not one ruler. The Torres Strait Islanders are a separate people, gardeners and sailors linked to New Guinea.
- **The Europeans.** Manila galleons cross the north; Tasman's voyages of 1642–44 are the VOC's last word on the south.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
- **Mana.** The setting's Oceanic name for Prime (Magic, Prime and the Threshold): spiritual power, authority and prestige, inherited, and gained or lost through action. On Pohnpei chiefly sacred power is *manaman* or *wu*.
- **Pohnpei builds with spells.** Olisihpa and Olosohpa raised Nan Madol's basalt; the druids and clerics who followed have kept it and built on it since. They know other ways to build and don't need them. Ceremonies at stone altars, *pei*, secure the land and sea at three ritual centers: Nan Madol, Salapwuk and Wene.
- **Wayfinding is a science:** it is an instrument panel of swells, stars, birds and clouds, taught in ranked, initiated schools. A Carolinian master navigator and a European navigator do the same job by different means.
- **Experts.** A Māori *tohunga* is an expert, not only a priest: of chant, carving, genealogy, healing. Illness is often broken tapu or *mākutu*, sorcery. Hawaiian *kāhuna* include healers and harmful sorcerers.
- **Australia's healers.** The *ngangkari* of the Central Desert treat harms to a person's spirit. The making of "clever" men and women is restricted knowledge and stays off the page.
- **The sea's otherworlds.** Pulotu and Hawaiki lie across the sea, not up or down: the Sea a Revelator of the Oceanus walks (The Plenum).

> **Further in.** Mana can be lost through action. Nobody in Europe has asked whether Prime can.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Each people has its own Hidden, almost all written down in the 19th and 20th centuries and projected back, and much of what is known is restricted by rank, gender, initiation or clan.

- **The patupaiarehe** (Aotearoa). The closest Pacific figure to the Hidden: a people of the misty hilltops with their own chiefs, fair-skinned, red- or fair-haired and never tattooed. Their flutes entrance a woman and can call her back at will. Dawn defeats them; firelight, cooking smoke and red ochre keep them off. They taught people netting, string games and sorcery, and red-haired families are said to descend from them.
- **The ponaturi.** Red-haired, white-skinned sea fairies with long claws, under the sea by day and ashore by night.
- **Taniwha.** Guardians or dangers of particular rivers, lakes and seas, closer to dragons than fairies (unverified).
- **The menehune** (Hawaiʻi). Night builders of walls and fishponds who must finish by dawn. One scholar argued the "little people" image came after contact and *manahune* first meant commoners; in 1668 a table can have either.
- **Eni** (Pohnpei). Spirits of the sky, land, ocean and mangroves, ancestral spirits and personal guardians: gods, ancestors and owners of places, not a fairy people.
- **Place spirits** (New Guinea and the islands). Owners of a pool, waterfall or river bend, tied to particular clans, appearing as snakes or crocodiles.
- **Country isn't the Hidden.** The Dreaming is Law and ongoing creation, not an otherworld, and mapping it onto the Hidden misrepresents it. The Kuninjku have made the Mimih public: escarpment spirits so thin the wind can snap their necks, who taught ceremony, hunting and rock painting.
- **No edge in Country.** The village edge doesn't fit Aboriginal Country, where every place is someone's home ground. It fits Aotearoa only from inside: the patupaiarehe's hills were the edges of Māori settlement, but still Māori land.

> **Further in.** One of the patupaiarehe's names, *Pakepakehā*, may be the source of *Pākehā*, the Māori word for Europeans.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **Guam.** The Jesuit San Vitores is bound for the Marianas to begin Spain's first continuous presence among the Chamorro; in our history thirty years of war follow.
- **Pohnpei** is forty years past the Saudeleur, under its chiefdoms.
- **Aotearoa.** Pā-building in the Waikato has paused; in our history it resumes with new fighting in the early 1700s.
- **Australia.** Whether Makassar trepang fishers have reached Arnhem Land yet is the DM's call.
- **Hawaiʻi, Tonga, Tahiti and Rapa Nui** have no Europeans.
- **The Monsoon Road** reaches this far, and its agents have put Wisdom-built places on their list.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The mission.** San Vitores's baptisms, a chief named Matapang and how long the peace lasts.
- **The method.** Monsoon Road traders asking how the stones were raised, and whether the method can be bought.
- **The fortified hills.** The Waikato's pā are quiet, and the fighting that ends the quiet is not far off.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The flute.** A patupaiarehe is heard on a misty ridge, and a woman keeps walking toward it. Her family wants her home; the cooking fires are the only ward, and the mist is coming down.
- **A navigator for hire.** A Dutch captain wants a wayfinder for a passage his charts don't show, and the school he asks doesn't sell its knowledge.
- **The stones.** A trader off the Monsoon Road wants a Nahnmwarki's permission to see Nan Madol at night, and the samworo want to know who is paying him.
- **The castaways.** Two mutineers were marooned among the Nhanta in 1629 and never seen again. A VOC surveyor wants to know what they told the Nhanta, and the Nhanta may want to know what he's looking for.

sections.heading: At a Glance
sections.text:
From the Volga to the Pacific and up to the Arctic shore, the empires of Russia, China and Persia meet peoples who have run this ground for millennia. In 1668 Uzbek khans rule the oasis cities, Kazakh khans and judges govern the grassland, the Dzungars run a Buddhist steppe state with cannon, a Mongol khanate holds the mouth of the Volga and Russia's fur collectors have reached the Pacific. The steppe's monsters are real, too: the little beaked beasts the griffin legends grew from are alive here.

**The one thing to remember:** there is no edge here. Herders and reindeer peoples move through their whole country on a planned round, and the spirits live where the people do. Every empire is trying to fix them in place, and none has managed it.

> **Further in.** Norilsk, one of the few places on earth that could match Mutapa's platinum, lies under the tundra at the edge of Russia's fur tribute. Nobody has looked.

sections.heading: The Lay of the Land
sections.text:
Every pasture here has its seasonal users, and moving between them is planned, negotiated and remembered.

- **The grass sea.** About 5,000 miles of grassland and semi-desert from the Black Sea to Manchuria (unverified). Herders move between summer and winter pastures on ancestral routes and hold reserve pastures in common.
- **The zud** is the winter disaster that kills the herds: deep snow over the grass (white), no snow and no water (black), a thaw that refreezes into ice the animals can't break (iron) or cold that burns them out. The answer is *otor*, an emergency move onto a distant community's reserve pasture, calling in an old debt.
- **The Gobi and the mountains.** The Tian Shan, with wild apple forests; the Gobi's bare rock and gravel, with wild camels, wild asses and the last truly wild horses on Dzungar land. Its red sandstones are rich fossil beds, where *Protoceratops*, sheep-sized, beaked and frilled, is common (unverified).
- **The oases.** Bukhara and Samarkand on the Zarafshan, Khiva in Khwarazm, which became the capital around 1600 after a branch of the Amu Darya dried up.
- **Siberia.** Taiga, larch on permafrost, bog, tundra and the coldest inhabited places in the world. The rivers are the roads: boats in summer, sledges on the ice in winter.
- **The Arctic.** Sea ice, bowhead and walrus, and Inuit engineering: the kayak, the toggling harpoon, houses with cold-trap entrances. In Sápmi many Sámi are shifting from hunting wild reindeer to herding them.

> *"Your map leaves this slope blank. Write my grandfather's name on it."* (a Kazakh herder to a Russian surveyor)

sections.heading: Who Holds Power
sections.text:
- **The Uzbek khanates.** Chinggisid khans in the oasis cities, with tribal amirs rising behind the throne. In Bukhara a *quriltai* elects the Janid khan and Naqshbandi Sufi shaykhs confirm him; the Juybari shaykhs are the richest landholders. Khiva is a slave market for Persian captives.
- **The Kazakhs.** Three *zhuz*, Senior, Middle and Junior, under Chinggisid khans and sultans, with *biys*, judges of customary law whose rulings are kept orally. Their capital is Turkistan, at the shrine of Ahmed Yasawi.
- **The Dzungars.** The western Mongol (Oirat) khanate, founded 1634 and ruled in 1668 by Sengge from the Ili valley around Ghulja (unverified): Buddhist, under the 1640 Oirat–Khalkha code, a state that mines metals, makes its own gunpowder weapons and farms as well as herds. Sengge's younger brother has been a monk in Lhasa since childhood.
- **The Kalmyks.** Oirats who rode west in the 1630s and took the lower Volga from the Nogais: a Buddhist khanate around Russian Astrakhan, at the mouth of Europe's greatest river, allied with Russia and in touch with the Dalai Lama.
- **Russia.** River forts from Tobolsk to Yakutsk and Okhotsk, on the Pacific, collect *yasak*, fur tribute, from every Indigenous man aged 18 to 50, often through hostages; Sakha leaders help collect it from their neighbors. The Nenets raid the collectors, and the Chukchi beat them in the field.
- **The Qing** to the east. The Khalkha Mongols haven't yet submitted, and the Russian–Qing border is undrawn.
- **The North Atlantic.** Three crowns tax the same Sámi households. Greenland has Kalaallit, Dutch whalers and no colony.
- **Every empire has its conquered.** The Kazakhs and then the Kalmyks pushed the Nogais west, Khiva sells Persians and the Sakha tax their neighbors for the tsar.

sections.heading: Magic Here
sections.text:
- **The Buddhist campaign against shamans** is live in 1668. Late-16th-century Mongol law banned shamanizing and the *ongon*, images that house ancestor and helping spirits, and burned them in public. Monks have taken over the shamans' healing and fees, and shamans hold out in the northern forests; the mountain, hearth and *ovoo* cults were never banned, and lamas wrote liturgies for them.
- **Learned magic.** Bukhara "the Noble" is a city of madrasas and of the Islamic science of letters (Magic, Learned Magic).
- **Healers.** Kazakh *baksy* and the women called *parikhon*, "peri-reciters," work with peri and jinn as helpers (unverified).
- **The Siberian shaman.** The English word is Evenki. A dead shaman's spirit chooses the next, usually a descendant, with an illness that won't end until the call is accepted. The shaman retrieves stolen souls, escorts the dead and defends the clan, in a fringed costume hung with iron and antlers; Evenki shamans aren't paid and are often poor. The three worlds the shaman travels hang on the Tree a Revelator of Yggdrasil walks (The Plenum).
- **The noaidi.** Sámi households keep painted drums for divination and decisions. Denmark–Norway made drumming a capital crime in 1609, and seized drums end up in princely cabinets.
- **The naturalist.** A Central Asian naturalist or druid is the first to study the steppe's little monsters as animals rather than legends. Paleontologists argued in 2024 that the griffin legend has nothing to do with *Protoceratops*; in Euphonia the beasts are alive, so the argument is settled differently.
- **Disease.** Smallpox has reached Siberian peoples since the 1630s; healers are few, and a magical cure leaves no immunity.

sections.heading: The Hidden Here
sections.text:
Herders and reindeer peoples have no village and no wild. Much of this was recorded in the 19th and 20th centuries, and Buddhism, Islam and Orthodoxy have reclassified many of these beings.

- **The *ezen*** (Mongol). "Owners" of a mountain, spring, lake or pasture, who sicken those who pollute water, dig, cut trees or kill wantonly. Mountains go by epithets because their names are dangerous (unverified). Travelers add a stone to the *ovoo* at a pass.
- **The *albasty*** (Kazakh, Kyrgyz and others). A childbirth demon with long tangled hair, who steals a mother's lungs; if she throws them into flowing water, the woman dies. A specialist drives her off by announcing "a hero has arrived," and seizing a strand of her hair gives power over her.
- **Peri.** Beautiful beings who take human lovers and possess the chosen: the nearest match here to European fairies, and the source of the English "peri." The cover's Persian elf is one. (The jinn are what Islam says they are, and not Hidden.)
- **The underground people** (Sámi). The *gufihtar* or *ulda* live under the hills, keep fine reindeer herds and exchange children; the *saivo* is a mirror world of spirit people a noaidi can visit (unverified). Close kin to the Scandinavian *huldufólk*.
- **The Tuniit** (Inuit). A strong, shy people who held the land before the Inuit and were driven out; archaeologists identify them with the Dorset culture (unverified).
- **Killers and the Hunt.** Where there's no village, riders, guards and the people themselves do the watching, and to herders the Wild Hunt looks like raiders. Keep clear of the European and Chinese default of steppe horsemen as a horde out of nowhere: here the steppe's own riders ride out against the Hunt.

> **Further in.** Siberians told Europeans the mammoth lived underground and died if it saw daylight (unverified). Its tusks are dug from the riverbanks and sold south every year.

sections.heading: What's Happening in 1668
sections.text:
- **The Dzungars** are under Sengge. In our history he's murdered in 1670, and the monk in Lhasa comes home.
- **The Kalmyks** are about to get Ayuka, who makes them a military power (1669 or 1672; sources differ).
- **The Kazakhs** have been fighting the Dzungars since the 1640s, with no single khan over all three zhuz.
- **Bukhara and Khiva.** About 500 Indian merchant-bankers lend from Bukhara's caravanserais. In Khiva the scholar-khan Abu'l-Ghazi died about 1664, and his son is finishing his history of the Turks.
- **Siberia.** Sable tribute has fallen from up to 22 pelts a man to about 3, and the frontier keeps moving east; furs are more than a tenth of Russia's revenue. The exiled archpriest Avvakum is about to write one of the first accounts of a Siberian shaman's séance.
- **The North.** Sweden's great witch panic begins. An English-financed voyage sails for Hudson Bay. The Chukchi are undefeated.

sections.heading: Trouble Brewing
sections.text:
- **The succession.** Sengge's rivals are close, and his brother in Lhasa is bound by a vow.
- **The tribute.** The sable is running out and the forts keep their hostages anyway.
- **The red alert.** The hunt for Mutapa's metal hasn't turned north yet.

sections.heading: Hooks
sections.text:
- **The specimen.** A naturalist has a live griffin-kin, and buyers in Bukhara, Moscow and London want it before anyone works out what it eats.
- **The hostage.** A clan leader's son is held at a Russian fort until the furs come in, and this year's furs won't.
- **The drum.** A Sámi household's drum is on its way to a princely cabinet, and the family can no longer make the decisions it was kept for.
- **The iron winter.** A zud has come, and a herding camp moves on *otor* to a pasture whose owners say the old debt was paid.
